title.narrative: R4.1: Number of Disease Prevention Assistants (DPAs) trained in delivering vector borne disease prevention and health messaging intervention

comment.narrative: The decision to train only 90 Direct Participation Agents (DPAs) was strategically made to optimize the program's effectiveness and efficiency. Originally, the plan was to train 430 DPAs, each working half a day per week. However, discussions with community members and Camp Committees highlighted that increasing the number of days each DPA worked per week would significantly boost their motivation and performance. Consequently, although fewer DPAs were trained, they were able to cover the same number of households—9,250—by working four days per week, which also allowed for more consistent and continuous engagement with the communities. This approach not only maintained the reach of the initiative but also reduced costs and logistical challenges associated with training a larger number of DPAs. Furthermore, it decreased the overall time required for training prior to implementation and helped mitigate the risk of spreading Covid-19 by limiting the number of trainees gathered at any one time

A 1,500-liter plastic tank was also installed on the roof of the bathrooms to enhance water storage and availability for sanitation purposes. The water network was connected from the main line to the health facility's internal network, ensuring a reliable supply of water. The incinerator at the health facility was rehabilitated, which is crucial for the safe disposal of medical waste, thus maintaining hygiene and preventing contamination. To support the facility's ongoing cleanliness and maintenance, cleaning materials were provided. This action served 3,574 individuals. The rehabilitation of Alghurafi Health Facility (HF) in Alghurafi Village, Almashalehah subdistrict, Al Mokha district, was focused on addressing key infrastructural issues and enhancing the facility's water management systems. Key interventions included fixing water leakage issues in the sewage pipes, which was crucial for maintaining sanitation and preventing potential health risks. Additionally, extensive maintenance work was performed on both the external and internal water networks, including the reconnection of pipes, to ensure a consistent and reliable water supply. To support the facility's water needs, a 5,000-liter plastic tank was installed to provide a dependable source of drinking water. Furthermore, a dynamo was supplied and installed to facilitate the efficient pumping of water from the ground tank to the upper tank, ensuring the availability of water throughout the facility. Another 1,500-liter plastic tank was installed on the roof of the bathrooms, further improving water storage and accessibility for hygiene and sanitation purposes. The rehabilitation also included the restoration of two manholes and the replacement of old drainage pipes with new ones extending to the sludge pit, which is essential for proper waste management. Additionally, the upper water tanks were maintained and cleaned, ensuring that the stored water remained safe for use. This action served 4,327 individuals. The rehabilitation of Jesr Alhamily Health Facility (HF) in Jesr Al-Hamily village, Alahmool subdistrict, Mawza district, involved significant upgrades to the facility's water and sanitation infrastructure. The project included comprehensive maintenance and rehabilitation of both the water and sewage networks, ensuring that the systems functioned efficiently and reliably. This work was crucial for maintaining hygiene standards and preventing contamination. Additionally, two large plastic water tanks, each with a capacity of 10,000 liters, were supplied and installed. These tanks provide a stable and adequate water supply for the facility, essential for both daily operations and emergency needs. A water flow meter was also installed, complete with a tap and an inspection room, to monitor water usage and ensure the efficient management of resources. Furthermore, the main gate door of the health facility was supplied and installed, which not only improves security but also enhances the facility's overall infrastructure. These improvements are designed to provide a safer, more hygienic, and better-equipped environment for healthcare delivery, benefiting both the staff and the community members who rely on the facility for medical services. This action served 637 individuals.

Consequently, the ongoing construction of latrines, which is expected to be completed in the coming months, will play a significant role in achieving this indicator.

During KAP2, two sites with a huge caseload of households (1800), contributing to a substantial sample size (182) in KAP1, were excluded, leading to deviations in the final results.
Moving forward, the SI HP team plans to enhance relevant health hygiene promotion messages during sensitization activities to address and improve these KAP indicators in the future

This positive result reinforces our belief that targeted interventions can significantly impact community health practices. (Refer Annex 8 and 9)

The value of this indicator was derived from endline surveys conducted between March and April 2024, encompassing both new and old villages. (Refer to Annexes 8 & 9)
The objective for this indicator was to achieve 80% compliance with sustainable safe hygiene behaviors, yet SI reached 71%. While this is a notable accomplishment, the shortfall highlights several key challenges. This includes the complexity of the hygiene practices, and the slow adoption rates. The effectiveness of such behavioral changes typically improves over time with continued education, reinforcement, and support.
This indicator is measured based on adherence to five specific handwashing criteria. Many individuals within our target community face difficulties in meeting these criteria, largely due to a high rate of individuals lacking formal education. This educational gap significantly impedes their ability to understand and consistently adopt these hygiene practices.
Changing established behaviors and instilling new hygiene practices in a population with limited educational backgrounds is inherently challenging and time-consuming. Although efforts were made to educate and promote these practices, the deep-seated need for sustained educational interventions and support means that behavior change is gradual.
Additionally, there are notable differences in outcomes between women and men. Compliance rates for safe hygiene behaviors are 81% for women compared to 36% for men, resulting in a weighted average of 71%. This disparity suggests that men may require additional and tailored educational sessions to achieve meaningful behavior change, which would ultimately impact the overall results.

In addition, as became apparent during the first entomological survey, people store their water in small jerry cans and water buckets rather than larger water containers, such as water drums. The SumiLarv 2MR disks can only be used in water containers of 40L upwards. While mosquitoes still breed in jerry cans and water buckets; these reciprocals are not suitable for the 2MR disks. As a result, the SumiLarv disks could not be used.

title.narrative: R2-2.3 % of households that dispose of their non-excreta waste in a safe way

comment.narrative:
The value of this indicator was derived from endline surveys conducted between March and April 2024, encompassing both new and old villages. (Refer to Annexes 8 & 9)
The overall achievement for Indicator 2.3, which measures the percentage of households disposing of their non-excreta waste safely, fell slightly short of the 80% target, reaching 78%. This shortfall is primarily due to significant regional disparities in performance.
In Al Khawkhah, only 62% of households were reported to dispose of their non-excreta waste safely. Survey results reveal that 37.6% of households leave garbage in public areas, 32.1% bury or burn it, and only 14.7% use designated disposal areas. These unsafe practices highlight the lack of adequate waste disposal infrastructure, poor socioeconomic conditions, and limited education in the region. Despite efforts to raise awareness, changing behaviors in a short period proved challenging. The awareness campaigns in Al Khawkhah were shorter compared to those in Mawza and Mokha, where the implementation started earlier and took longer, resulting in better outcomes.
Conversely, higher percentages in Mawza, Mokha (both 84%), and the new villages (90%) suggest that when resources, and sustained awareness programs are in place, households are more likely to engage in safe waste disposal practices. These areas benefited from effective community engagement, and longer-term interventions.
